title: Bronchiolitis and Infant Respiratory Distress: Assessment and Admission Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Clinical diagnosis, severity assessment, supportive care and disposition for babies and children with bronchiolitis.
findings: Rebuilt against the approved-topic structure: a tiered investigation panel, time-ordered management and an explicit medicine decision pathway.
Every investigation row includes a reference or normal state, condition finding and next action.
Previous outline and published rows remain preserved; this additive version is pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: No topic-specific Saudi national guideline was found in the opened Saudi Ministry of Health protocol index unless a Saudi source is explicitly cited in the medicine row.
Current live Saudi Food and Drug Authority product registration was not individually confirmed; clinicians must check the hospital formulary.
Local antibiogram, resistance pattern, shared-care agreement and imaging availability require site-level confirmation where relevant.

pathophysiology.summary: Viral inflammation and mucus obstruct small airways. Air trapping and atelectasis impair gas exchange. Young infants can fatigue, feed poorly and develop apnoea.
keyMechanisms: Viral inflammation and mucus obstruct small airways.
Air trapping and atelectasis impair gas exchange.
Young infants can fatigue, feed poorly and develop apnoea.

references.title: NICE NG9: Bronchiolitis in children—diagnosis and management

symptoms: Coryzal prodrome followed by cough, tachypnoea, feeding difficulty and wheeze or crackles.
physicalSigns: Increased respiratory effort, recession, nasal flaring, crackles or wheeze and reduced intake.
redFlags: Apnoea, cyanosis, severe distress, exhaustion, reduced consciousness, dehydration or persistent low oxygen saturation.
precipitants: Respiratory viral infection; severity risk is higher in very young or premature infants and those with chronic lung, cardiac, neuromuscular or immune disease.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Recurrent episodic wheeze without crackles, especially in an older infant/child.
High fever or persistently focal crackles.
Sudden onset or focal unilateral findings.
Hepatomegaly, murmur, poor growth or pulmonary oedema pattern.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Coryzal prodrome for 1–3 days followed by persistent cough plus tachypnoea or recession and wheeze or crackles (NG9 1.1).

ruleIn.normalValue: Oxygen saturation at least 92% in air
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistent saturation below the age/risk admission threshold
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Measure in every child; interpret with work of breathing, feeding, age and comorbidity.

ruleIn.testName: Respiratory rate and work of breathing
ruleIn.normalValue: Age-appropriate rate without recession, grunting or apnoea
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Tachypnoea, recession, grunting, exhaustion or apnoea
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines severity and need for admission or respiratory support.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced intake, dehydration or inability to feed safely
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines oral, nasogastric or intravenous fluid support.

ruleIn.testName: Apnoea observation in young or high-risk infants
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Apnoea is an admission and escalation feature even without marked wheeze.

ruleIn.testName: Blood gas in impending respiratory failure
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Reserve for severe deterioration; do not use routinely.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph only when an alternative diagnosis or intensive care is considered
ruleOut.normalValue: No focal consolidation, collapse or air leak
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine radiography can mimic pneumonia and lead to unnecessary antibiotics.

ruleOut.testName: Viral testing only for cohorting or local infection-control need
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Does not usually change individual treatment; follow local infection-control policy.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess breathing and feeding
actions: Record oxygen saturation, work of breathing, apnoea history, hydration and risk factors.
Escalate apnoea, exhaustion, cyanosis or severe distress to paediatric critical care.

clinicalManagement.title: Provide supportive care
actions: Use minimal handling and nasal suction only when secretions impair breathing or feeding.
Provide enteral or intravenous isotonic fluid when oral intake is inadequate according to the paediatric fluid pathway.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose admission or discharge
actions: Admit when oxygenation, apnoea, hydration, work of breathing, risk factors or caregiver/social circumstances make home care unsafe.
Do not use antibiotics, bronchodilators, adrenaline or corticosteroids routinely for bronchiolitis.

medicationPlan.note: Routine salbutamol, ipratropium, corticosteroids, nebulised adrenaline and antibiotics are not indicated for bronchiolitis. Management is supportive: oxygen when the guideline threshold is met, suction when secretions impair feeding or breathing, and enteral or intravenous fluids when intake is inadequate.

teaching.scope: Clinical diagnosis, severity assessment, supportive care and disposition for babies and children with bronchiolitis.
learningObjectives: Recognise the condition and its red flags.
Choose initial tests without delaying urgent escalation.
Use a named multidisciplinary disposition plan.
keyPoints: Apnoea, cyanosis, severe distress, exhaustion, reduced consciousness, dehydration or persistent low oxygen saturation.
Admit when oxygenation, apnoea, hydration, work of breathing, risk factors or caregiver/social circumstances make home care unsafe.
pitfalls: Stopping after a short outline instead of documenting the full investigation pathway.
Using a medicine row without checking the branch, allergy, organ function, culture result and local formulary.
Mistaking publication status for clinical approval; this version remains pending until a clinician approves it.

patientEducation: Explain the working diagnosis, immediate plan and specific return or deterioration signs.
lifestyleAndDiet: Address prevention and self-management only after the acute safety plan is complete.
dischargeCriteria: Clinically stable, maintaining age/risk-appropriate oxygen saturation in air, taking adequate fluids and caregivers understand red flags.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Give return advice for apnoea, cyanosis, worsening effort, exhaustion or poor intake; arrange review for high-risk infants as locally required.
